newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia Parliament passes new privatisation law.
newsitem.headline: Serbia Parliament passes new privatisation law.

text.p: Serbia's parliament adopted on Monday a landmark privatisation law paving the way for attracting foreign investment to a market economy and setting up the ownership structure in almost 5,000 medium and small companies.
The 250-seat parliament voted 117 for the law with 10 against and five abstaining. The opposition, which holds the remaining seats, is boycotting the parliament.
"(The law) is adopted although there have been many doubts," Serbian Privatisation Minister Milan Beko told Reuters after the bill was passed. He added: "We are on our way."
Beko said his ministry would need around $10 million for the first year to implement the privatisation process.
He said he expected technical help from Britain and from the Italian government via the Finest joint Yugo-Italian financing venture.
"We have asked the French bourse to deliver software for the central depository stock account," Beko said.
Serbia's Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic said the right environment existed for privatisation to begin.
"Today.. with $1,600 per capita income, high growth rate and with price and dinar stability we are completely ready to transform our economy in full.
"With the ownership transformation law, Serbia's government is rounding up years of activity aimed at creating a modern market economy," he told the parliament before the vote.
Beko said privatisation, although not compulsory, would be inevitable. He said the state was there to create a legal framework within which market mechanisms will be set free.

The law, effective from October 31, leaves companies to decide whether to privatise. It envisages heavy discounts for shares distributed to between four and five million workers, pensioners and farmers.

Workers and pensioners of privatised firms will be entitled to a dinar equivalent of shares worth 400 German marks for each year of service. Farmers will enjoy the same right for each year of fully paid social insurance.
Shares up to 6,000 marks in value will be eligible for a 20 percent basic discount plus one percent for each year of service. Larger amounts will not carry a discount.
"Discounts are effective one year from the day a company decides to privatise," Beko said.
Before privatisation starts, ten percent of the capital in all companies to be sold will be transferred to the Serbian Pension Fund.
Fifty percent of privatisation receipts will go to the Serbian Development Fund and 25 percent each to the Pension Fund and to Serbia's Labour Market Office.
No money will go to special funds to service the state's $4 billion debt to citizens for hard currency savings frozen in 1991, Beko said.
Instead, holders of frozen savings will be able to swap their hard currency deposits for shares in companies that will be privatised.

"The law creates a new economic civilisation... a new environment, management structure, good motivation for foreign investments, improved allocation of resources, strengthens competition and breaks monopolies," Beko said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254
